title: Agenda: Matthew and Cyrus, Wednesday 2026-11-04, noon Mountain
sub: The topics Matthew brings to his meeting with Cyrus on Wednesday 2026-11-04 at noon Mountain time (12:00 MST, Boulder), in three parts: performance, Hazel embedded in JS programs, and DSL tile editors as livelits. A work in progress: compiled over the two days before the meeting and updated as items move, so each item says where it stands, as of when, and what it needs from the meeting.
short: Performance: an edit and an undo each cost time in proportion to the program, and an undo about three edits. Measured on #2635 at five sizes: at 6,400 definitions an edit takes about 106 ms and an undo about 292, each followed by about 78 ms of statics. Two cheap fixes are on #2635 and took 31 to 46% off at the larger sizes; what is left is whole-program passes around incremental caches that already work. Getting to O(log n) is a design question for the meeting (^report(36), in progress).

Hazlets: Hazel embedded in a JS program's event handlers. A new word for the pattern Messed Up Dress Up uses, the first and so far only one. A demo of the game's scripts, the question ^report(34) asks (should the library be official?), and a prototype npm package, hazeljs 0.0.1, published on npm on 2026-11-02.

DSL tile editors as a kind of livelit: Matthew's proposal. The livelit's literal is a Hazel value describing a grammar, its view is a tile editor for that grammar, and its expansion is the parse tree. Is this the shape Cyrus wants, and what should the first demo be?

sections.title: 1. Performance, and the cost of undo
sections.intro: What an edit and an undo cost as programs grow, and the questions next to it. Measured in Node on #2635 (livelits × modular editors). The report on undo is ^report(36); the series is ^report(35) and before.

items.title: Undo in O(log n)? What an edit and an undo cost now
items.body:
Measured: a program of n top-level definitions (let v1 = v0 + 1 in …), an edit in the middle one, then undos and redos, each through the app's own update loop. From 400 to 6,400 definitions every step grows in proportion to n. At 6,400, after the fixes: an edit about 106 ms, an undo 292, a redo 184 (medians of 12), each followed by about 78 ms of statics. An undo costs about three edits and a redo about two; about 26 ms of each is the outline, rebuilt from scratch on every undo and redo. The undo history itself (push, pop, compacted snapshots) is not where the time goes.

Why it is linear: the incremental caches work (each step parses 1 or 2 definitions again, re-measures 1 or 2 chunks, compares 2 definitions' heads in statics), but around them are passes over every definition: rebuilding the top-level term, statics' walk down the chain of definitions, the outline (rebuilt on every undo and redo), layout's walk.

Fixed, on #2635 (394552d5d0, bfa36a6ede, pushed 2026-11-02): the auto-probe recomputed the whole top level's skeleton every frame, and completion suggestions were computed after every typed digit. 31 to 46% off each step at 3,200 and 6,400 definitions.
items.meeting: O(log n) per edit and per undo needs the top level as a balanced tree of definitions, not a chain of nested lets: each node keeps summaries (the names its subtree binds, its rows, its part of the skeleton), so each pass touches only the edited definition's path, and a snapshot shares every other node, so an undo can be a swap of roots. Is that the direction, and how much of it is worth doing before the livelits land?

items.title: How much sharing is lost passing data to and from the eval worker
items.body: Values cross to the worker and back by Marshal, with ShareCodec's tables on both sides sending a value already sent as a reference (993e3d5f91, 2b080af683). Still lost: small values, first sends, everything after a table reset; and every value decoded on the page is a new object, so the page's identity-keyed memos miss on it and hash it again. To measure per request and response: bytes with and without sharing, hit rate, encode, decode and hash time, for a slider release, a Full Body edit and an undo.
items.meeting: Worth measuring before the meeting, or after the undo design?

sections.title: 2. Hazlets: Hazel embedded in a JS program
sections.intro: Hazlet, our shorthand from here on: Hazel embedded as a library within the event-handler system of a JavaScript program, so that some of the program's handlers are Hazel functions it calls with events and whose results it acts on. Messed Up Dress Up (MUDU), the game Matthew makes with M and N, is the canonical example, and so far the only one: five of its rooms hand their events to Hazel rules, on_event : (Globals, Event) -> Cmd, through a draft library, hazel-lib.js (#2711, with #2719 stacked on it). ^report(33) is a case study of those rules; ^report(34) asks whether the library should be official.

items.title: A demo: MUDU's game scripts
items.body: The game, live at matthewhammer.org/kids-choice-games/dress-up/: its Scripting tab, where a room's rule is written in Hazel, in Fumola or in JS and runs as the room's event handler. ^report(32) times the game loading and checking every script in each of the three. ^report(33) reads what the rules meet today (a per-room view of the game, not its state) and proposes names for every place and thing, and types built on them.
items.meeting: Cyrus's read of the rules' types, and of what a Hazlet should give its handlers: a view built per room, as today, or the program's whole state under readable names?

items.title: Should the library be official?
items.body: ^report(34)'s suggestion: merge #2711 and #2719 as an experimental library, built on dev and labelled so; promise stability only for the small core (analyze, run, the value mapping) once a second Hazlet besides MUDU has used it.
items.meeting: Merge as experimental, yes or no; and who else might build the second Hazlet?

items.title: A prototype npm package: hazeljs
items.body:
A task for Claude: what it takes to publish a prototype npm package that anyone can install and use, documented the way npm packages are. Split into linked tickets: the package's build for node and the browser (^ticket(669)), TypeScript declarations (^ticket(670)), the README and a CHANGELOG (^ticket(671)), examples and an install check on GitHub (^ticket(672)), the name, license, versions and who publishes (^ticket(673)), and MUDU loading its Hazel from the published package (^ticket(674)).

A first version, the same day: hazeljs 0.0.1 (the name is Matthew's pick; Hazlet stays the name of the pattern), built from #2719 at 0d66c36618: hazel-lib.js, entry points for require and import and a browser script tag, TypeScript declarations, and a README the npm way, which sends readers to hazel.org and to the GitHub contributors for who makes Hazel. 648.5 kB packed (2.8 MB unpacked). Installed from its tarball into a fresh project, every example in the README runs. Found on the way: a module of about 150 members overflows Node's default stack, and the ms field always reads 0; both are in the README's limits.

Published 2026-11-02 at 11:03 MST, under Matthew's npm account: npmjs.com/package/hazeljs, so npm install hazeljs works. Checked from the registry, not the tarball: a fresh project installs it and runs the README's examples through require and import, and jsDelivr and unpkg both serve hazel-lib.js for a script tag. npm also lists a placeholder it made first, 0.0.0-stage, to be deprecated. Not done yet: the browser and TypeScript examples, the install check on GitHub, and MUDU loading its Hazel from the package.

Matthew's next ask: the trap room live in ^report(34), its Hazel rule editable in Hazel's tiles and the room answering each edit (^ticket(675)); not started.
items.meeting: Keep it under Matthew's npm account, or move it to a Hazel organization on npm (@hazelgrove)? And is the package the library alone, or also the Hazlet pattern: a helper that turns a program of modules into JS event handlers, as MUDU uses it?

sections.title: 3. DSL tile editors as a kind of livelit
sections.intro: Matthew's proposal, for discussion: a new kind of livelit, perhaps built in, for languages defined inside Hazel.

items.title: A livelit whose literal is a grammar and whose view is a tile editor for it
items.body:
• The literal is a Hazel datatype describing a context-free grammar: its production rules.
  • Behind the scenes, a parser generator reads that grammar. Menhir is one candidate; a simpler generator could come first if needed.
  • The livelit's model, view and update present a tile-based editor for those production rules.
  • The expansion is the program's abstract syntax as a parse tree, as a Hazel value, or something analogous.

Related so far. Cyrus's interest in DSLs in Hazel as tile-based livelits, and his pointer to language boxes (Diekmann and Tratt's Eco editor: each box has its own lexer and parser, and is one token to its parent) for #2542, the shared-tokenizer limit on sub-language tiles. Fumola as tiles: a sort in Hazel's own tile grammar (#2529), and ^fumola_wip on the remote-splices branch (2026-09-29), a livelit that edits Fumola code as tiles, a first prototype of a DSL as a tile livelit. Hazel's own tiles come from a fixed table of forms in its source (src/haz3lcore/lang/Form.re); this would make the grammar a value a program writes.

A question the parser raises: Menhir generates OCaml code when Hazel is built, so on its own it cannot read a grammar written in a running program. A grammar given at run time needs a parser built at run time, such as an Earley parser, which accepts any context-free grammar, or tables built in the browser. Or the grammar's definition could be compiled ahead of time for built-in DSLs only.
items.meeting: Is this the shape Cyrus has in mind for DSLs in Hazel? Built-in, or user-defined livelits? Grammars given at run time, or compiled ahead of time? And what is the first demo: a small grammar (arithmetic, or a JSON-like data language), its tile editor, and its expansion as a Hazel value?
